The Council Chambers can accommodate a maximum of 30 participants, at which point the general public
may address the Planning Commission on an agenda item by waiting in the City Hall Court Yard and
entering the Chambers one at a time. No one will be admitted into the Council Chambers who is ill or
exhibiting symptoms of COVID-19. The Planning Commission is not accepting live comments
electronically at this time.

The public can submit written comments prior to 3:00 p.m. on the day of the meeting in person to the
Planning Department at City Hall or via email to dromo@cityofavalon.com.

Staff reports for each agenda item are posted a minimum of 72 hours prior to the meeting and are available
for review in person or on the City website at http://www.cityofavalon.com.

 In compliance with the Americans with Disability Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this
 meeting, please contact Denise Radde, City Clerk (310) 510-0220. Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting
 will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. (28 CFR 35.
 102-35.104 ADA Title II). All public records relating to an agenda item on this agenda are available for the

  STAFF REPORT – PC# 2818

  Application File: Site Plan; CEQA.
Item No. 2 – General Business  Submitted by: Susanna Gutierrez, Planning Dept.

Project Name: Application for a Site Plan for a minor addition to an existing single family
dwelling at 371 Whittley Avenue

Project Description: An application for a Site Plan for an 85 square foot infill addition to an
existing single family dwelling in the Low Density Residential zone. The project is in the Coastal
Zone but exempt from a Coastal Development Permit, as well as State CEQA guidelines per
Section 15301 - Existing facilities. The Planning Commission will determine whether the project
is within the 300-foot appealable seaward area boundary. The associated entitlements require
Planning Commission review but no public hearing.

  Owner/Applicant:  Richard Denney (Dr. Denney)
  Location:  371 Whittley Avenue
  APN:  7480-025-014
  PC#:  2818
  Zone:  Low Density Residential (LDR)
  File Date:  09-29-2022

Page 1 of 6
 Discussion:

  The project site itself
  involves an irregularly
  shaped parcel measuring
  9,674  square  feet,
  surrounded  by  other
  residential lots of various
  shapes/sizes in the Low
  Density Residential zone
  (LDR). Located at 371
  (upper)  Whittley,  the
  property is characterized by
  the street’s intersection with
  Las Lomas Drive and
  Marilla Avenue, as well as
  nearby  higher  density
  residential  development.
  (note: area not to scale)

The 1,595SF single family dwelling was originally built in 1928 and contains a total of three
bedrooms and two bathrooms. Due to the slope of the lot, the main floor/entrance fronts Whittley
Ave, while the change in elevation accommodates two stories in the back. The lower level
foundation begins just above the double retaining walls on Marilla and is mostly visible from the
street, albeit much higher than the standard line of sight. In contrast, heavy landscaping and
decorative walls significant impede visibility from the Whittley street side. The area of expansion
is also partially obscured by the covered entryway/patio.

This application proposes to incorporate
an additional 85SF of living space to the
main level set back from Whittley
Avenue behind the covered front entry
way. The expansion of the exterior walls
eliminates the existing concavity of the
first story and lines up exactly with the
structural footprint of the lower story.
The project relies heavily on floor to
ceiling window placement in the
direction of the bay and results in a more
consistent structural façade -essentially
filling in a “cut out” on the rear corner
closest to Marilla Ave. Despite a change in overall square footage, the scope of work does not
result in any additional bedrooms, kitchen, or bathrooms, and will be incorporated into the
existing floor plan.
Page 2 of 6
   GENERAL PLAN, LAND USE, AND ZONING COMPLIANCE

Annual Growth Policy:
Staff recommends that the Planning Commission make the finding as required by the 2022
Growth Policy that the proposed remodel will not have any growth inducing effect and does not
create the need for additional employees, thus the project is allowed by the 2022 Growth Policy.
As residential use intensity is measured by dwelling units/acre, and the existing density is not
changing, there should be no change in intensity. The growth policy provides that new
development will only be permitted for the following classes of projects and almost all require
confirmation from SCE that adequate fresh water is available:
  1. The repair, in-kind replacement, remodeling or enlargement of existing commercial
  and residential structures, subject to specified conditions;

Site Plan:

A site plan approval is required since the project doesn’t qualify as a “minor renovation” per
municipal code section 9-3.613(b). AMC Section 9-8.203 requires that the Site Plan be approved
based upon three (3) factors and principles. These criteria and the corresponding explanation of
project compliance are as follows:

  (a) Every use, development of land and application of development standards shall take
  place in compliance with all applicable provisions of this title. The proposed project
  does not have any foreseeable effect on the use or development standards associated
  with this property. As the intensity of residential use is measured by dwelling
  units/acre, and the existing density (1 unit – SFD) is not changing, there should be no
  change in intensity. The addition will be incorporated into existing living space and no
  bedrooms/bathrooms/kitchens will be created.

  (b) Every use, development of land and application of development standards shall be
  considered on the basis of the suitability of the site for the particular use or
  development in-tended, and the total development, including the application of
  prescribed development standards, shall be so arranged as to avoid traffic
  congestion, insure the protection of public health, safety and general welfare, prevent
  adverse effects on neighboring property and shall be in general accord with all
  elements of the General Plan. As discussed, the scope of work is limited to a minor
  addition that does not protrude from the farthest points of the existing structural
  footprint (no expanded building envelope) with a protected line of site along the main
  access road (Whittley Ave.).The applicant will need to follow standard building permit
  requirements and meet all applicable codes, ensuring a minimal effect on neighboring
  properties.

  (c) Every use, development of land, application of development standards shall be
  considered on the basis of suitable and functional development design, but is not
  intended that such approval be interpreted to require a particular style or type of
  architecture. The design of the proposed remodel is suitable for a single family

   residential structure and will have minimal effect on the architectural style of the
  building. The project relies heavily on floor to ceiling windows facing the bay and
  results in a more consistent structural façade -essentially filling in a “cut out” on the
  rear corner closest to Marilla Ave.

  ENVIRONMENTAL DETERMINATION

CEQA:

The project is Categorically Exempt under Section 15301(a) CEQA Guidelines-Existing
Facilities, which exempts the following:

(e) Additions to existing structures provided that the addition will not result in an increase of
  more than:
  1. 50 percent of the floor area of the structures before the addition, or 2,500 square feet,
  whichever is less

Coastal Development:

  All projects within the City of Avalon are located in
  the Coastal Zone. Under AMC 9-8.103(h), the
  Planning Commission must determine whether the
  project is within the 300 foot appealable seaward area
  boundary. Based on the appealable area map excerpt
  included, it is staff’s recommendation that the
  Planning Commission make the finding that the
  project is not within the 300 foot appealable zone.
  City staff determined the project to be exempt from a
  Coastal Development Permit according to Municipal
  Code section 9-8.102(b)(1), as an “improvement to an
  existing single-family residence” that does not fall
  into the three subcategories of “involving a risk of
  adverse environment effect,” codified below:

“Application. In addition to any other permits or approvals required by the City, a coastal
development permit shall be required prior to commencement of any development in the City,
except:

  b) Developments determined to be excluded from the coastal permit requirements as
  established in Division 20, § 30610 of the Public Resources Code, as set forth below:
  1. Improvements to existing single-family residences except those classes of
  development which involve a risk of adverse environment effect, defined as:
  i. Improvements to single-family structure within 50 feet of the edge of a
  coastal bluff;
  ii. The expansion or construction of water wells or septic systems;

  the sea or within 30 feet of the inland extent of any beach or of the mean
  high tide of the sea where there is no beach, whichever is the greatest
  distance, improvement that would result in …”

Fresh Water Availability (SCE): The scope of work does not contribute to the creation of an
additional bedroom or bathroom, which is considered to be exempt from needing a Fresh Water

Recommendations:

Based on the findings, Staff recommends the Planning Commission:

  1. Find the project categorically exempt under CEQA Section 15301, Class 1 – Existing

  2. Find the application exempt from Coastal Development Permit and make the determination
  that the project is not within the 300-foot appealable zone; and
  3. Approve the Site Plan as proposed with all applicable entitlements incorporated, subject to
  the standard list of conditions
  4. Find the application allowed under the 2022 Growth Policy.

Option: The Commission may impose additional conditions as are deemed necessary at the time

BACKGROUND

Project Title: Application for a Transient Rental License and Coastal Development Permit
located at 67 Playa Azul Hamilton Cove.

Project Description:

Request for approval of a Transient Rental License and Coastal Development Permit to allow the
renting or leasing of a room or rooms for periods of fewer than thirty (30) consecutive days
duration located within a single family residence The unit consists of two (2) bedrooms and two
(2) bathrooms. The project is in the Coastal Zone and subject to a Coastal Development Permit,
which requires a public hearing and Planning Commission approval. The Planning Commission
will determine whether the project is within the 300-foot appealable seaward area boundary.
The project is Categorically Exempt under Section 15305 of the State CEQA Guidelines – Minor
Alterations in Land Use Limitations.

  Owner/Applicant:  Kathleen Streeter and Kim Wooden
  ADDRESS:  67 Playa Azul, Building # 10
  APN:  7480-048-085
  PC #:  2813

The Avalon Municipal Code (“AMC”) § 3-1.310(e)(5) provides that the Planning Commission
shall consider, “whether granting the Transient Rental License shall result in any year round
residence located adjacent to the proposed transient rental having more than a majority of the
adjacent residences permitted or licensed for transient rental use…”. Upon analysis, the
saturation map below indicates that less than 50 % of the properties adjacent to 67 Playa Azul,
Building # 10 hold either conditional use permits or Transient Rental licenses.

 Saturation Map:

I have not provided a saturation map because more than 60% of the Condominiums at Hamilton Cove
are designated as transient rentals.

Floor Plan: The property is part of building 10 and is located on the 1 st floor of the complex. The
unit has two (2) bedrooms and two (2) bathrooms

Property Manager/24 Hour Contact: The property manager Hamilton Cove Property
Management Ph., 310-510-0190 and the 24 hour contact 310-750-7743.

GROWTH POLICY

Southern California Edison (SCE) has determined the conversion to a transient rental will not
require a water allocation; thus, the application is in compliance with the 2022 Growth Policy.

CEQA REVIEW

The proposed project is Categorically Exempt under Section 15305 of the State CEQA
Guidelines - Minor Alterations in Land Use Limitations (i.e., CUP for transient rental) which do
not result in changes in land use or density.

DISCUSSION

The proposed project involves a request of approval for a transient rental application for a
transient rental license under Article 3 of the AMC Transient rental use is permitted in any
zone upon Planning Commission approval of a Transient Rental License. (AMC 9-6.602(a)) The
house has been previously used as a vacation home for family and friends.

COASTAL DEVELOPMENT PERMIT:

In December 2016, the City received an opinion letter from the California Coastal Commission
(Coastal Commission) noting their position that conversion to transient use constitutes a
change in intensity in use and should be authorized pursuant to a coastal development permit.
Based on the opinion, the application for transient rental use must include a Coastal
Development Permit (CDP).

The project is in the Coastal Zone and is subject to a Coastal Development Permit, which
requires a public hearing and Planning Commission approval. Specifically, the project requires
a Coastal Development Permit under Section 9-8.102(b)(2)(v) of the AMC, as the proposed
project seeks to allow the renting or leasing of a room or rooms with or without table boards
for periods of fewer than thirty (30) consecutive days duration (Transient Rental – Section 9-
6.602 (a) of the AMC) at 67 Playa Azul.

 Under AMC 9-8.103(h), the Planning Commission must determine whether the project is
within the 300-foot appealable area boundary. Based on the appealable area map excerpt
included below, it is staff’s recommendation that the Planning Commission make the finding
that the project is within the 300-foot appealable zone.

An appeal of the Planning Commission’s Coastal Development Permit action may be filed with
the City Council within fifteen (15) days after mailed notice of the action to the applicant. Any
person may appeal the Planning Commission’s determination that a proposed project is
seaward of the appealable seaward area boundary to the Coastal Commission, and following
exhaustion of local appeals, any aggrieved person may appeal actions on local Coastal
Development Permits seaward of the appealable area boundary to the Coastal Commission.

The proposed change in use conforms to the certified Local Coastal Plan (AMC 9-8.103(d) (1))
because it increases access of the public to the coastal zone. For the Planning Commission to
issue a Coastal Development Permit, the Avalon Municipal Code requires that the Planning
Commission make certain findings. These findings and corresponding explanations of the

   BACKGROUND

Summary

AB 2221 and SB 897 are the latest legislative moves in this direction. Both bills will take effect on Jan. 1,
2023. When they do, any local ordinance will be null and void if it does not conform to AB 2221’s and SB
897’s changes to state ADU law. To avoid this result, local agencies should update their ADU ordinances
before Jan. 1, 2023.

AB 2221 and SB 897, both of which amended Gov. Code section 65852.2, include numerous changes to
the state ADU laws. There are two dominant themes in the changes. First, cities must let ADUs go taller
and closer to the property lines. Second, the Legislature codified a number of interpretations of the law that
agencies developed as they’ve interpreted and applied the ADU law in different situations over the last few
years.

Height Limitations - local agencies must allow ADUs taller than 16 feet in the following circumstances:

•  If it is located within a half-mile of a major transit stop or high quality transit corridor, a detached ADU
  that is on a lot with a single-family or multifamily dwelling may be up to 18 feet in height by right, and
  the ADU be up to two feet taller (for a maximum of 20 feet) if necessary to match the roof pitch of the
  ADU to that of the main house. Before this most recent legislation, local agencies could cap the height
  of a detached ADU at 16 feet.
•  If a detached ADU is on a lot with an existing or proposed multistory multifamily dwelling, the ADU
  may be up to 18 feet in height (again, by right), regardless of how close it is to transit.
•  An attached ADU may now be up to 25 feet high or as high as a primary dwelling may be under the
  underlying zone, whichever is lower. But a city may still limit the ADU to two stories.

Front Setbacks

Cities have authority to impose front-yard setbacks on ADUs that are subject to an ADU permit, and that
remains generally true, but now a front setback must yield to the extent necessary to enable the construction
of an 800 square foot ADU with four-foot side- and rear-yard setbacks. The law has included a similar
“must yield” provision for FAR, lot coverage and open-space requirements; the Legislature has added front
setbacks to that list.

Adjustments to Application Review Procedures; Additional Restrictions on Denials

•  If a city denies an ADU application, it must now provide the applicant with a “full set of comments”
  listing the specific items that are “defective or deficient.” These comments must also describe “how the
  application can be remedied” by the applicant. Most cities have been doing this already in practice.
•  A demolition permit for a detached garage that is to be replaced with an ADU must now be reviewed
  with the ADU application and issued at the same time. Many cities have already been doing this in
  practice, too.
•  Local agencies cannot deny an application to create an ADU solely because corrections are needed to
  address nonconforming zoning conditions, building code violations, or unpermitted structures
  elsewhere on the lot that do not present a threat to public health and safety and are not affected by the
  construction of the ADU. Not many cities have been attempting to do this since the ADU law already

  2
   required cities to disregard nonconforming zoning conditions and building code violations to a great
  extent when considering an ADU. But note that this is only a limit on holding up an ADU to require
  compliance elsewhere on the property; it does not insulate the property owner from having to come
  into compliance separately from the ADU.

Expansion of Where JADUs Can be Built; New Configuration Requirements

•  Under existing state law, a junior accessory dwelling unit (JADU) must be “within the walls” of a
  proposed or existing single-family dwelling. In light of HCD commentary, most cities have understood
  this to include nonlivable space within the primary dwelling structure, such as attached garages. Now
  the Legislature has made that express. The new amendments specify that “enclosed uses within the
  residence, such as attached garages, are considered part of the proposed or existing single-family
  residence.” This is more a change in the text of the law (that needs to be reflected in the local ordinance)
  than it is a substantive change in what the law requires. Most cities have already been doing this.
•  In instances where the JADU shares a bathroom with the primary dwelling, local agencies must now
  require the JADU to have an interior entry to the primary dwelling’s “main living area,” independent
  of the exterior entrances of the JADU and primary dwelling. This too is something that has widely been
  done in practice but is now an express requirement in the law.

Meaning of “Objective”

Lastly, most cities have understood what the law means by objective standards (based on other changes to
housing law in recent years), but the Legislature has now inserted an express definition into the ADU law:
An “objective” standard as a standard that involves “no personal or subjective judgment by a public official”
and that is “uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark or criterion available
and knowable by both the development applicant or proponent and the public official prior to submittal.”

Next Steps

Because state law requires complete, across-the-board consistency between a local ordinance and the state
ADU law, nearly every — if not every — city and county in the state with an ADU ordinance will once
again need to amend its ordinance to comply with the changes above. Failure to do so by Jan. 1, 2023, will
render any nonconforming local ordinance null and void.

submitted to the City and is found to be in compliance with State law and City zoning regulations (to the
extent they don’t conflict with State law), the City must issue Planning approval and Building Permits upon
